messages.content:
You are checking one scene of a novel for one specific continuity error.

The book had already established this, earlier or elsewhere:
- (a08-what-the-folk-fear) "Tallow's lantern swung from a hook on his belt, throwing their shadows long and strange against the bark. He had not spoken since they left Wick's darkened house."

A past rewrite of this scene contradicted it. The error looked like this:
- (a06-standing-guard) "The old Folk woman worked without speaking, her hands quick and sure"
- (a06-standing-guard) "Tallow stood beside her with her arms folded and her small lined face sharp."
(Summary: a06 makes Tallow an old Folk woman (she/her), but a08 and a09 have Tallow as he/him.)

Here is a NEW draft of the same scene:
<scene>
By the fourth night, Nora knew the path.

She knew where the roots crossed the trail like sleeping cats, and where the Old Oak threw its big dark shadow, and which lanterns among the roots burned low and which burned bright. She knew the little voices now, too, the way you know a song you have heard many times. She could pick out Wick's from across the whole village, high and glad, calling her name before she was halfway down the slope.

Leo knew none of it. He walked a step behind her with his hands half-raised, as if the dark might reach out and he would have to catch it.

"You don't have to come," she told him again, soft so the Folk wouldn't hear her being unkind. "I can hear them. You just stand there."

"I stand there so you can hear them," Leo said.

That was the whole of it, with Leo. He had said he would guard her, back on the night of the pledge, and now he guarded her like a wall guards a door, close and flat and always between her and whatever he didn't like.

Tonight he didn't like the hollow.

It lay at the far edge of the village, past Tallow's woodpile, where the lantern-light thinned out to almost nothing. A single lamp burned there, down among the cold stones, and it was guttering. Nora heard it before she saw it. A small sound, the smallest she had ever heard a flame make, like a child trying not to cry in the next room.

She went toward it.

"Nora." Leo's voice, low.

"There's one down there. It's crying, Leo, I can hear it crying."

She was already moving, already picking her steps between the stones, her hands out for the little lamp. She had done this three nights running. She had cupped her hands around guttering flames and said the warm things the Folk said to each other, and twice the little lights had steadied and grown. She was good at it. She was the only one in the whole wide world who could do it, and she knew it the way she knew her own name.

Leo stepped in front of her.

He didn't say anything. He just put himself there, between her and the hollow, his back to the thinning light, so that she had to stop or walk into him.

"Move," she said.

"It's too dark down there."

"That's where it is. That's where the crying is."

"Then let Tallow carry a lantern to it."

"Tallow can't hear it. I can hear it." She tried to go around him and he shifted, quick for someone so big, and stayed in front of her. "Leo. Let me."

"No."

Up by the woodpile, Tallow lifted his head. He was a broad, square sort of Folk, with a voice like a door closing, and he had been sorting wet kindling from dry since they came. He watched the two of them for a moment and said nothing, which was Tallow's way of saying a great deal.

A new lamp bobbed up over the stones. Pip. Pip was smaller than Wick even, and newer, and he had taken a shine to Nora the way a moth takes a shine to a window. He stood at the edge of the hollow with his little light held high, peering down into the dark toward the crying.

"It's going out," Pip said, in his thread of a voice. "It's going out, Nora."

She looked at Leo. His face was the one he wore when he had decided a thing and would not un-decide it, shut like a fist.

"Watch the trees, then," Nora said, and when he turned his head, just for a breath, to do the thing she had told him to do — she went.

She didn't go toward the hollow. She let him think she might, and then she slipped sideways, light and quick, down and around the far side of the woodpile where his big shoulders couldn't fit. Pip ran ahead of her with his lamp, lighting the way down into the stones.

"Nora!"

She heard him come after her, heard the scrape and crash of him trying to take the path she'd taken and not fitting it, and she almost laughed, because she had been right, she had known best, and here was the little crying lamp just below her now, small and blue and nearly gone. She knelt. She put her hands around it the way she had learned.

"There," she whispered. "There now. I've got you."

Leo's hand closed on her sleeve.

She didn't feel the pull as a pull. She felt the world tip. One moment she was kneeling in the last of the light with the little flame in her hands, and the next her own weight was going the wrong way, dragged sideways and back, her knee skidding off the cold stone, her hands flying open and empty.

She went into the dark.

It wasn't like stepping into shade. The warmth went out of her all at once, out of her face and her fingers and the backs of her arms, as if the night had opened its mouth around her and breathed in. She couldn't see them. She could feel them. Cold pressing close on every side, cold with a kind of weight to it, cold that wanted the little bit of warm that was her.

Somewhere far away Pip's lamp was a small gold coin and getting smaller.

Then Tallow's voice, sharp as a snapped stick: "Pip. Her hand. Now."

A grip on her wrist. Small fingers, a child's fingers, and strong. Pip hauled, and Tallow shouted again, and Nora scrabbled with her feet against the stones and came up and up out of the cold, back toward the coin of light, which grew and grew until it was a lamp again and then a whole ring of lamps, and she fell into the middle of them on her hands and knees in the warm.

She knelt there a while, breathing.

Her left arm was cold to the bone. She rubbed it with her other hand and it stayed cold, a deep down cold that the lamplight couldn't reach, and when she looked at the skin in the gold glow it had a grey look to it, dim, like a coal gone out.

Leo stood a little way off. His hand was still half-closed, at his side, holding a fistful of nothing.

Nora wouldn't look at him. She looked at her cold grey arm and rubbed it and rubbed it.

"I was right there, Leo," she said. Her voice came out small and even, which was worse than shouting. "I had it."

"You were falling," Leo said.

"Only because you grabbed me."

Down in the hollow the little crying lamp had gone silent. Not steadied. Silent. She knew what that meant now and she didn't let herself look.

Tallow came and stood between the two children, square and solid, his own lamp on the ground beside him. He tilted his head back to take in all of Leo, the whole tall shape of him against the dark.

"She was not falling, big one," Tallow said. "She was walking."

Leo opened his mouth. Nothing came out of it.

Pip had Nora's cold wrist in both his small hands and was chafing it between them, his little face screwed up with the work of it, his own light flickering with the effort. "It'll come back," he was saying, to himself as much as to her. "It'll come back, the warm comes back, it does."

Nora watched Pip's hands move on her grey arm.

She did not look up at her brother at all.

</scene>

Does the new draft make the same error — does it assert something that contradicts what was established, in the way described? A draft that simply leaves the fact out does not make the error.

Answer with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"verdict": "reintroduced" | "consistent" | "not_present", "evidence": "<verbatim sentence from the new draft that decides it, or empty for not_present>"}

"reintroduced": the new draft contradicts the established fact.
"consistent": the new draft states the fact and agrees with what was established.
"not_present": the new draft does not touch the fact either way.

content.text: {"verdict": "consistent", "evidence": "He was a broad, square sort of Folk, with a voice like a door closing, and he had been sorting wet kindling from dry since they came."}
